# Differences Between Accuracy, Error, Tolerance, and Uncertainty in a Calibration Results. Now in this article, I will present the differences, relationships, and Interpretations of the following terms: Accuracy, Tolerance, Error, and Uncertainty. 4. The relationships between Accuracy, Error, Tolerance, and Uncertainty in Calibration Results. **Uncertainty** is the ‘range of values’ where the true value or actual location of the measurement results (UUC) lie, while the **Error** is the ‘exact result’ of the difference between the UUC and STD which shows how accurate the measurement result is by showing the actual distance to the true (STD) value. Calibration tolerance limits are provided by the user, by regulatory bodies, or as per specifications, while Uncertainty is calculated based on the combined errors related to the STD and UUC. **The Relationships Between Accuracy, Error, Tolerance, and Uncertainty – The Interpretation from a Calibration Result**. While accuracy is calculated based on error and true value, **Uncertainty** is calculated based on the combined errors or inaccuracy of reference standards (STD) and the Unit Under Calibration (UUC). The Relationships Between Accuracy, Error, Tolerance, and Uncertainty from a calibration results. **The Relationships Between Accuracy, Error, Tolerance, and Uncertainty from a calibration results**. 4. The relationships between Accuracy, Error, Tolerance, and Uncertainty from a Calibration Results. There are other methods in which you will use the TUR, where you will use the tolerance limit of the torque screwdriver, and the measurement uncertainty of the transducer, but this method requires that your instrument is calibrated with a measurement uncertainty result. About error and uncertainty, what we add is the measurement uncertainty and the measured value and then we compare it to the tolerance. Once you have that uncertainty value, you can now use the formula for TUR which is **TUR=tolerance limit/measurement uncertainty** (0.20/uncertainty). You can use the manufacturer accuracy of ‘0.02% of reading’ to calculate TUR with the same principle but the measurement uncertainty is more advisable since more error contributors are considered. If you are using the decision rule, you need to add (or subtract) the measurement uncertainty in the UUT reading, then check if it is within the tolerance limit.

results.title: Calibration uncertainty in molecular dating analyses: there is no substitute for the prior evaluation of time priors | Proceedings B | The Royal Society
results.content: Crucially, our results demonstrate that: (i) *a posteriori* methods have led to the recurrent selection of erroneous constraints, and (ii) the effective time priors implemented in an analysis differ for individual calibrations when employed alone or in variable combinations with additional constraints—this means that estimates of calibration quality based on consistency do not provide a faithful indication of how a given calibration will impact the analysis in combination with others. Non-uniform priors express approximations of divergence timing relative to a minimum constraint, however, such calibrations are rarely evidence-based [13]. For each individual calibration, during each round of cross-validation, the tree was calibrated using a single uniform calibration prior, with a hard minimum and soft maximum constraint based on fossil evidence [27]. Increasing the uncertainty in the timing of divergence relative to fossil minima, based on a non-uniform prior, led to an increase in both prior and posterior age estimates across all nodes (figure 1; electronic supplementary material, table S1). Analysis without sequence data demonstrates that the specified calibration priors are not faithfully implemented in the joint estimation of divergence times. In all contemporary Bayesian molecular clock programs, the initial specified calibration priors will not be the same as the effective calibration priors actually implemented in the estimation of divergence times [12,13,30,32,35]. The results of our analyses identify two additional and ultimately fatal problems with the cross-validation approach: (i) cross-validation methods demonstrably result in the selection of calibrations that are not supported by the available fossil evidence (table 1), and (ii) this approach is compromised within the Bayesian framework because the effective priors for a given calibration vary depending on the presence or the absence of other constraints (figure 3). Consequently, different combinations of calibrations, in combination with the tree prior, will produce different joint time prior constructs—this occurs regardless of the (non-uniform or uniform) prior probability densities employed, or the approach used (directly or indirectly) to specify the (soft) maximum constraints. Bayesian estimation of species divergence times under a molecular clock using multiple fossil calibrations with soft bounds. A likelihood method for assessing molecular divergence time estimates and the placement of fossil calibrations. Assessing the quality of molecular divergence time estimates by fossil calibrations and fossil-based model selection.

results.title: A Primer on Uncertainty and Calibration in Deep Learning
results.content:
Title: A Primer on Uncertainty and Calibration in Deep Learning
Hence, uncertainty in deep learning is the **lack of confidence a model has in its predictions**, typically arising from **incomplete information, ambiguous data, or limitations in the model itself** (this shouldn’t be confused with confidence value model gives as output, though ideally it should, this discrepancy in expected and actual behaviour of model logits/probability/scores is comes under model calibration, this also will be covered in latter sections). 2. **Epistemic uncertainty** (model-level): captured by `p(θ∣D)`, i.e., the uncertainty in model parameters due to limited or non-representative training data. A deterministic model makes a point prediction `y=f(x`), but a probabilistic or uncertainty-aware model outputs a **distribution** over possible predictions: `y∼p(y∣x).`. Here, instead of a fixed variance (ideally), the model predicts **input-dependent variance** (`σ term)`, which captures **aleatoric uncertainty**. Unlike aleatoric, epistemic uncertainty **can be reduced**  by gathering more data, improving the model, or training on diverse distributions. This simplest way of modelling this type of uncertainty is by predicting not just a mean output `μ(x)` but also a corresponding variance `σ2(x)`, treating the output as a Gaussian distribution:. Compared to CNNs or RNNs, LLMs operate in a **higher abstraction space**, which means uncertainty isn’t just about data or model exposure , it’s also about **semantic alignment, factual grounding, and reasoning calibration**. This idea leads us directly to the concept of **model calibration**, which is less about what the model predicts, and more about how much faith we should place in those predictions, its very similar to uncertainty itself, but has a subtle difference. Uncertainty refers to the model’s *own belief* about how confident it is in its predictions of a sample. So, while uncertainty describes **what the model thinks**, calibration evaluates **how well that belief aligns with reality,** it’s like a local/sample-level vs global/dataset-level behaviour. A model can express high uncertainty (e.g., a uniform distribution), but still be poorly calibrated if its estimated probabilities don't match observed outcomes. Conversely, a model may express confident predictions (low uncertainty) but be overconfident and hence **badly mis-calibrated**. This kind of uncertainty isn't intrinsic to the task or the model’s knowledge; instead, it **emerges from what we do to the model post-training**, particularly from techniques like **quantization**, **weight pruning**, **low-rank approximations**, and **hardware-constrained inference**.
